newsitem.title: USA: TALKING POINT - Campbell Soup restructure.
newsitem.headline: TALKING POINT - Campbell Soup restructure.

text.p: Campbell Soup Co's efforts to boost profits through a financial and operational restructuring can pay off in a mature industry where strong growth is hard to achieve, analysts said.
"The bottom line is that we expect earnings to improve," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Tim Ramey, in raising his rating on Campbell stock to buy from hold.
Said Paine Webber analyst George Staphos, "They hit on several themes that are important for food companies in terms of how they can control earnings over time."
"I think their track record is good and much of what they're working on should be theoretically controllable," he said. "I think the prospects are good."

Campbell announced earlier that it had authorized a $2.5 billion stock repurchase program, was planning to divest businesses representing $500 million in annual sales, and would trim costs by $200 million annually over two years.
Cost cuts would include 650 job reductions, including 175 at its Camden, New Jersey headquarters.
Around midday, Campbell shares were up 4-3/8 from Wednesday's close on the New York Stock Exchange, at 71-7/8.

Campbell also said it was buying from Grand Metropolitan Plc soup maker Erasco Group of Germany, which Campbell said was the leading soup maker in the largest soup market outside of the United States.

Analysts said Campbell chairman David Johnson told a meeting in New York Campbell aimed to steadily improve earnings while increasing sales growth from current levels of about three to four percent annually.
"What he'd like to see is sales growth on the order of eight percent," said Fourteen Research analyst Sally Schaadt.
Ramey said earnings growth targets appeared to be around 15-16 percent annually, compared with 15 percent in the year to July 1996 and about 11-13 percent in previous years.
Debt used to finance the share repurchase would raise the company's debt level to about 16 percent of capital from a current nine percent -- "not what I would call heavy leverage," Schaadt said.

Ramey estimated in his report the first stage of the share repurchase, a $1.5 billion "dutch auction," could boost earnings by $0.05 a share. Cost savings could add another $0.50 to $0.60 a share by the fiscal year to July 1988.
However, Ramey told Reuters, some of those savings would be plowed back into the business through acqusitions and supporting their core brands.
He said Campbell planned to sharply increase advertising spending.
Campbell told the analysts company that officers and employees have agreed not to participate in the Dutch auction, Schaadt said.
They could not provide similar assurances with respect to the Dorrance family, which controls some 58 percent of Campbell stock.
But at the meeting in New York, Johnson cited Campbell's strong record of dividend increases which had provided large shareholders with strong, growing income, Schaadt said.
In addition to Campbell's announced plans to sell its poultry operations, the company also "alluded" to the possibility of selling its Argentine beef operation, Ramey said.

Central to Johnson's strategy is his declared aim to move Campbell's financial performance into what he called the "Best of Show" category -- outpacing the entire food industry to perform in the top ranks of branded consumer goods firms.
This may be a tall order given the maturity of the industry, Schaadt said.

But plans to continue seeking expansion of the soup market -- such as through the introduction of a premium line of soups in glass jars -- indicate that Campbell is thinking along the right lines, she said.
"If the market itself can be expanded, he (Johnson) is going to get most of it," she said.
